lead: Touch gives VR two channels at once. One sits in the skin and reports contact, edges, stretch and vibration. The other sits in muscles, tendons and joints and reports where the limb is, how fast it moves and how hard it pushes. A designer who knows which receptor carries which signal can pick the right actuator, the right pin pitch and the right frequency band instead of guessing. The same numbers decide whether a pin array, a vibration motor or a force-feedback arm is worth its cost in a surgical trainer, a training simulator or a phone.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.6 for the device families.

blocks.text: Touch is two senses. When you lift a steel tumbler, the cutaneous system in the skin reports contact: pressure, edges, stretch and vibration. The kinesthetic system in muscles, tendons and joints reports the limb itself: position, speed and force. Most VR systems feed only the skin, so the user feels contact but never weight.

Mechanoreceptors are nerve endings in the epidermis and dermis, the outer and middle layers of skin, sitting above a fat layer. Two words classify them. Slow adapting (SA) receptors keep firing while a stimulus is held. Fast adapting (RA) receptors fire when the stimulus changes and fall silent when it is steady. Type I has a small receptive field near the surface; type II has a large field deeper down.

sections.h3: Density, two-point threshold and pin pitch

blocks.text: Receptor density is not uniform. The fingertip pad carries the highest density of Merkel and Meissner endings in the body; the palm has far fewer, the back of the hand and the forearm fewer still. Density sets the two-point discrimination threshold: the smallest gap at which two simultaneous touches feel like two points rather than one. It is about 2 to 3 mm on the fingertip pad, about 10 mm on the palm and a few centimetres on the back. Touch your forearm with two pencil tips and move them apart to feel the threshold yourself.

This number fixes the pitch of a pin array, a plate of small pins that rise and fall to draw shapes on the skin. Pitch is the centre-to-centre distance between pins. Pins placed closer than the threshold land inside one sensory patch and cannot be told apart, so you pay for actuators and drive electronics and gain nothing. The rule is pitch ≈ threshold: 2 to 3 mm at the fingertip, around 10 mm for a palm patch. A refreshable Braille cell, at roughly 2.5 mm dot spacing, sits exactly at the fingertip limit.

blocks.where: N is the number of pins in a square array; L is the side length of the patch in mm; p is the pitch in mm; L/p is the number of intervals along one side; adding 1 gives the number of pins on that side, because n intervals need n + 1 pins.

sections.h3: The kinesthetic sense: length, force and angle

blocks.text: Muscle spindles lie parallel to the muscle fibres, wrapped in a small capsule with a sensory nerve around them. Stretching the muscle stretches the spindle, and its firing rate reports both muscle length and the speed of change. Golgi tendon organs sit where muscle meets tendon, in series with the fibres, and report force rather than length. Joint capsule receptors signal extreme angles and rotation speed, but most joint position sense comes from spindles and tendon organs combined. That combined sense is proprioception.

Proprioception is coarse next to touch. People match a joint angle to within a few degrees, roughly 2 to 5 degrees at the elbow, against 2 mm at the fingertip. Force is judged with a just-noticeable difference (JND) of roughly 5 to 10 percent: the force must change by that fraction of its base level to be felt. Stiffness is judged more coarsely still, at roughly 10 to 15 percent.

Three effects matter in design. Adaptation: a constant force fades within seconds, so a device holding a steady push feels weaker than it is. Masking: a strong vibration hides a weaker one nearby, so neighbouring pins should not run at similar frequencies. Cross-channel: vibration applied while the finger presses changes the perceived stiffness of the surface. The engineering payoff is a simple mapping from receptor to hardware.

items: Pacinian (RA-II): vibrotactile actuator at 200 to 300 Hz, for alarms, texture and contact events.
Merkel (SA-I): static pin displacement, for edges, shapes and Braille.
Meissner (RA-I): 5 to 50 Hz flutter, for slip and surface change.
Ruffini (SA-II): tangential skin stretch, for friction and grip cues.
Spindles and tendon organs: force or torque feedback, for weight and stiffness.

spec.aria: Two rows of pin positions along a 10 mm side: six pins from 0 to 10 mm at the 2 mm fingertip pitch giving 36 total, and three pins at the 5 mm palm pitch giving 9 total.

examples.question: A fingertip pad carries a square pin array of 1 cm × 1 cm with pins on a 2 mm pitch. How many pins does it need? A palm patch of the same 1 cm × 1 cm is built at 5 mm pitch, finer than the palm's 10 mm threshold but still much coarser than the fingertip's 2 mm. How many pins does the palm patch need, and how many times fewer is that?
steps: Side length L = 1 cm = 10 mm. Fingertip pitch p = 2 mm.
Pin positions along one side = 5 + 1 = 6, at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 mm.
Palm pitch p = 5 mm. Intervals along one side = 10/5 = 2.
Pin positions along one side = 2 + 1 = 3, so palm pins = 3 × 3 = 9.
Ratio = 36/9 = 4. The same area needs four times fewer pins at the coarser pitch.
examples.answer: 36 pins on the fingertip array and 9 on the palm patch, so the palm patch needs 4 times fewer pins for the same area.
examples.check:
L = 10
p_f = 2
p_p = 5
int_f = L // p_f
side_f = int_f + 1
n_f = side_f * side_f
int_p = L // p_p
side_p = int_p + 1
n_p = side_p * side_p
ratio = n_f // n_p
print(int_f)
print(side_f)
print(n_f)
print(int_p)
print(side_p)
print(n_p)
print(ratio)

traps: Treating the skin as equally sensitive everywhere: the array that feels sharp on a fingertip feels like one blank slab on the palm.
Confusing the two-point threshold with pin-array resolution, and confusing the interval count L/p with the pin count L/p + 1 along one side.
Swapping receptors: Pacinian (RA-II) carries 200 to 300 Hz vibration, Merkel (SA-I) carries steady pressure and edges, Ruffini carries stretch, Meissner carries flutter.
Assuming joint position sense comes only from joint capsule receptors; most of it comes from muscle spindles and tendon organs together.
Forgetting adaptation: a steady force cue fades within seconds, so any answer about holding a constant force in VR must mention it.

quiz.q: Which mechanoreceptor signals vibration near 200 to 300 Hz, and which signals steady pressure?
quiz.a: Pacinian (RA-II) signals 200 to 300 Hz vibration. Merkel (SA-I) signals steady pressure and fine edges.

quiz.q: Define the two-point discrimination threshold and give its value at the fingertip and at the palm.
quiz.a: It is the smallest gap at which two simultaneous touches are felt as two separate points. About 2 to 3 mm at the fingertip pad and about 10 mm at the palm.

quiz.q: Why does a 2 mm pin pitch waste actuators on the palm?
quiz.a: The palm threshold is about 10 mm, so pins 2 mm apart fall inside one sensory patch and the user feels a single blob. Since pin count goes as 1/p², a 2 mm pitch drives roughly 25 times as many pins as a 10 mm pitch over the same area, and about 6 times as many as a 5 mm pitch, with no gain in felt resolution. A pitch near 5 to 10 mm gives the same sensation with far fewer actuators.

quiz.q: Distinguish cutaneous from kinesthetic sensing, naming one receptor for each.
quiz.a: Cutaneous sensing is contact information from skin receptors, for example the Pacinian corpuscle reporting vibration. Kinesthetic sensing is limb state from receptors in muscles, tendons and joints, for example the muscle spindle reporting muscle length and its rate of change.

quiz.q: A square fingertip array is 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm with 3 mm pitch. Find the pins per side and the total number of pins.
quiz.a: L = 15 mm, p = 3 mm. Intervals = 15/3 = 5. Pins per side = 5 + 1 = 6. Total = 6 × 6 = 36 pins.

quiz.q: A palm patch is 2 cm × 2 cm with 5 mm pitch. Find the total pin count.
quiz.a: L = 20 mm, p = 5 mm. Intervals = 20/5 = 4. Pins per side = 4 + 1 = 5. Total = 5 × 5 = 25 pins.

quiz.q: A haptic glove must signal object slip and also object weight. Which receptors must each cue target, and which effect limits the design?
quiz.a: Slip is a change over time, so drive RA-I (Meissner) flutter at 5 to 50 Hz, helped by SA-II (Ruffini) tangential stretch for friction. Weight is a sustained force, so use a kinesthetic force-feedback mechanism that loads the tendons, targeting spindles and Golgi tendon organs. Adaptation limits the weight cue, since a held force fades within seconds and must be refreshed or modulated; masking limits the slip cue, since strong pins hide weak neighbours.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research rigs now pair a coarse kinesthetic exoskeleton with a dense fingertip array, because each channel covers what the other cannot. Ultrasonic mid-air haptics and electrotactile arrays try to remove the moving parts altogether. Neuromuscular stimulation aims to drive muscles directly through electrodes on the skin. Search for tactile acuity, vibrotactile masking and stiffness discrimination JND to go deeper.
